articles.headline: France's Borrowing Costs Hit 5%, a Number Last Seen in 2002
articles.dek: The 10-year yield briefly topped 5% as Paris tries to pass a budget through a parliament that cannot agree on lunch, let alone 54 billion euros in cuts.
articles.catch_up: France has been running a wide deficit and piling up debt while its parliament stays divided and its governments keep falling over budget fights. Protests that began last month as a Parisian student movement turned into weekend rioting.
articles.why_it_matters: When a government's borrowing costs rise, that expense eventually shows up in taxes, public services and the rates charged on loans across the economy. France is a core euro-zone economy, so doubts about its finances matter well beyond Paris.
body: The yield on France's benchmark 10-year government bond briefly crossed 5% on Wednesday for the first time since 2002, CNBC reported. It was later around 4.9794%, about 6 basis points higher on the day. Translation: a basis point is one hundredth of a percentage point, so the market moved a small amount in a direction that finance ministers dislike.

A bond yield is the annual return investors demand for lending to a government. When the yield rises, investors are asking for more money to hold the debt, usually because they think it is riskier. France is therefore being told, in the polite language of markets, that its customers would like a better deal.

The reasons are not obscure. France ended last year with a deficit of 5.1% of GDP, while the EU, which has placed the country under its excessive deficit procedure, recommends something closer to 3%. Translation: Brussels has opened a file on France for spending more than it should, and the file is getting thicker.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu says he will target 54 billion euros ($60.6 billion) in spending cuts in the 2027 budget. The difficulty is that cuts must pass a divided parliament, and CNBC noted that investors doubt such a body can agree on them. Past budget fights have toppled governments, and Lecornu himself resigned less than a month into his tenure, only to be reappointed by President Emmanuel Macron days later. This is one way to demonstrate continuity.

The government has a workaround. Finance minister Roland Lescure told RTL that ministers have what he called "guardrails," including Article 49.3 of the constitution, which lets the Prime Minister force a bill through the National Assembly without a vote. Lecornu used emergency legislation to push this year's budget through in February. Translation: if parliament cannot agree, the budget will proceed anyway, which solves the vote problem and leaves the confidence problem for another day.
Lescure said he was convinced the budget would pass because, in his words, "we have no choice." That is a candid summary of the bond market's position as well.

The street adds complications. Protests that started as a student movement last month turned violent, and officials estimate weekend rioting and looting caused damages worth hundreds of millions of euros. Unrest is awkward timing for a government trying to persuade citizens to accept austerity.

Next spring's presidential election looms as another source of uncertainty. Frontrunner Marine Le Pen said earlier this month she could bring the deficit below 3% within 18 months of taking office, though critics question whether her proposed savings are credible. Bond traders, who have heard many deficit promises, will presumably want to see the arithmetic.
The 5% line is a round number rather than a cliff, and the yield slipped back under it. But it gives headline writers something to point at, and the budget talks now have a very visible scoreboard.
articles.wire_headline: French 10-year bond yield hits 5% for first time since 2002 amid unrest

articles.headline: Housing Market Enters Deep Sleep as Fed Weighs Rate Hikes, Which Are Known Sleep Aids
articles.dek: Pending home sales hit a record low in data going back to 2001, mortgage rates sit near 7.4%, and the Fed's next move may be up.
articles.catch_up: Mortgage rates have climbed sharply over the past year while inflation has stayed stubborn, leaving the Federal Reserve with little room to help housing. New data from the National Association of Realtors and the Commerce Department show the market weakening further in September.
articles.why_it_matters: Anyone hoping to buy, sell, or refinance a home faces borrowing costs more than a full percentage point above last year's, with no relief scheduled. Because the Fed's attention is on inflation, housing is unlikely to get help soon.
body: The National Association of Realtors reported Tuesday that its pending home sales index, which counts homes under contract but not yet sold, fell 7.3% in September to the lowest level in records going back to 2001. It was down 11.3% from a year earlier. Wall Street had expected a decline of 0.4%, which is the sort of miss usually described as a surprise by people who were not trying to buy a house.

Translation: pending sales are a forward-looking measure, so they show what closings will look like in the coming weeks, not what already happened. A record low here is less a snapshot than a weather forecast, and the forecast is fog.

The Commerce Department added to the mood. According to CNBC, housing starts fell 5.2% in the month against an expected drop of 0.4%, and building permits slipped 0.2% when economists had penciled in a 2% gain. Single-family permits totaled 845,000, the lowest since 2023. Builder sentiment, CNBC noted, is at its weakest in 14 years.

The main culprit is the mortgage rate. CNBC reported that Mortgage News Daily had the 30-year rate above 7% for most of September and ending near 7.6%. Five years ago it was closer to 3%. The Mortgage Bankers Association's weekly survey showed a slight dip to 7.41% from 7.50%, its first decline in more than two months. Applications fell anyway: total volume dropped 5.3%, purchase applications fell 7%, and refinancing fell 2%.

This is where the lock-in effect comes in. Translation: homeowners with cheap old mortgages do not want to sell and trade them for expensive new ones, so they stay put, and fewer homes reach the market. Goldman Sachs economist Ronnie Walker noted that more than 95% of mortgage borrowers have rates below the current level, and 65% are at least 2 percentage points below. Goldman expects existing home sales of 3.9 million in 2027, about 26% below 2019 levels.

Some buyers are adapting. The MBA said adjustable-rate mortgages made up 10.5% of applications, with rates almost a full percentage point lower than the 30-year fixed. Translation: an ARM is a loan that starts cheap and later resets to whatever the market charges, which is a bet that the future will be kinder than the present.

The Fed cannot easily rescue anyone. Wholesale final demand goods prices rose 2.6%, the fastest pace in a data series dating to December 2009, according to CNBC. Fed officials are also watching price pressure from artificial intelligence investment, which is raising the cost of chips and electronics, though they believe that investment could offset weakness in sectors like housing. In other words, the plan for housing is that someone else's boom will cover it.

Markets expect the Fed to hold rates next week, but CME Group's FedWatch tool implies a strong chance of quarter-point hikes in December and March 2027. Chris Rupkey of Fwdbonds wrote that housing is heading for a deep freeze. The NAR's Lawrence Yun offered a counterpoint: because mortgage rates have risen far more than the Fed's own hikes, they may be topping out. Buyers and sellers, he said, may simply be waiting for better rates.
That is a fair description of the entire market at the moment: everyone is waiting for someone else to move first.
articles.wire_headline: Housing is flashing warning signs just as the Fed weighs more interest rate hikes

articles.headline: AI Bubble Gets 10% Odds on Polymarket, 100% Odds of Being Discussed at Lunch
articles.dek: Traders bet on a pre-New Year burst, Ken Griffin calls it a bubble but says keep holding, and neocloud executives insist rental prices are rising.
articles.catch_up: Investors have spent months debating whether AI spending has outrun AI profits. Neoclouds, firms that borrow heavily to buy Nvidia chips and rent out the computing power, are now the focus of that debate after stress showed up in CoreWeave's debt markets.
articles.why_it_matters: If AI computing capacity keeps renting at high prices, the debt behind the data center buildout looks manageable. If it does not, the pain would reach anyone whose index fund quietly became an AI fund, which is most people with a retirement account.
body: MarketWatch reported that traders on the prediction market Polymarket see roughly a 10% chance that the AI bubble bursts before New Year's Day. Translation: a prediction market is a place where people stake money on outcomes, so a number like 10% is the crowd's price for being right about disaster. It is a modest figure, which suggests the crowd is nervous but has a dinner reservation in December.

Separately, MarketWatch reported that Citadel's Ken Griffin thinks AI stocks are probably in a bubble, yet is not telling investors to dump them. This is a coherent position held by many professionals: the thing is overvalued, and also the thing may keep going up. Translation: he is describing the weather, not canceling the picnic.

The stress point is the neoclouds. CNBC reported that these companies are investing billions to buy Nvidia's graphics processing units (GPUs, the chips that train and run AI models), build data centers and rent out the capacity. Investors grew wary after the spread on CoreWeave's five-year credit default swaps reached levels generally viewed as signs of distress, and its bond yields climbed. Translation: a credit default swap is insurance against a borrower failing to pay, and when the insurance gets pricey, the market is quietly raising an eyebrow.

Enter the executives, who were reassuring. Nebius chief revenue officer Marc Boroditsky told CNBC that his firm is not in CoreWeave's position because it is not carrying that kind of debt. He said Nebius would sell out if it brought its 2027 capacity online, and that 2028 could look similar. Asked whether price per megawatt, which measures what a company can charge for a given amount of computing capacity, would keep rising faster than expected, he answered: "Yeah." It is the most efficient earnings-call answer on record, and also the one least likely to be audited.

Crusoe CEO Chase Lochmiller offered the sharper evidence. He said Crusoe sees higher prices for older A100 chips than in 2020 or 2021, and higher prices for H100s than when they were first deployed in 2023. This matters because investors have been arguing over how quickly GPUs lose economic value as newer chips arrive. If old chips rent for more, the borrowed money looks wiser. If the claim comes only from firms that sell the rentals, readers may wish to note who is holding the tape measure.

SpaceX supplied the day's lift. CNBC reported that SpaceX said revenue at its AI business jumped ninefold to $7.56 billion, and CFO Bret Johnsen said pricing is tracking slightly above the high end of a $30 to $50 per watt range. Nebius stock rose, and CoreWeave, Iren and Applied Digital gained in premarket trading. Boroditsky said supply continues to fall far behind demand, a sentence that is bullish when said by the people selling supply.

For context, SPY, the exchange-traded fund tracking the S&P 500, stood at 772.45 as of October 21, 2026. The bubble question, then, is being asked of an index that has plenty of room to fall. The 10% odds on Polymarket will be the number to watch, along with whether CoreWeave's insurance gets cheaper.
articles.wire_headline: Polymarket traders see a 10% chance the AI bubble bursts before New Year’s Day
